events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Great Schism of Christianity
events.blurb: The pope's legate and the patriarch of a Bosphorus capital excommunicated each other over a long-brewing dispute about papal authority, the phrasing of the Nicene Creed, and the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist. Mutual anathemas remained in force for 911 years. The Roman and Orthodox churches have never fully reunited.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 1054 — Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius. The excommunications were formally lifted in 1965 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras. The "filioque clause" dispute sounds obscure but was genuinely the trigger.

events.title: Saladin Retakes Jerusalem
events.blurb: A Kurdish Muslim sultan, having crushed a Crusader field army three months earlier at the Horns of Hattin, accepted the peaceful surrender of the holy city from its desperate defenders after an eight-day siege. In contrast to the bloody Frankish sack of the city 88 years earlier, he permitted ransomed Christians to leave with their possessions and freed many who could not pay. News of the fall triggered the Third Crusade.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1187 — Saladin. His reputation for chivalry, magnified by his later adversary Richard the Lionheart, made him a hero of medieval European literature despite being its opponent. Dante placed him in Limbo rather than Hell.

events.title: Black Death Reaches Europe
events.blurb: A plague arriving by trade galley at a Sicilian port spread through Mediterranean shipping lanes and overland caravans until, over the next five years, it killed an estimated 30-60 percent of Europe's population — perhaps 50 million people. Physicians had no effective response; flagellant processions and mass pogroms of Jews did little but spread the disease faster.
events.revealBlurb: October 1347 — Messina, Sicily. Caused by Yersinia pestis, spread by the fleas of black rats. Wages for surviving laborers roughly doubled; labor scarcity began eroding feudal obligations. The plague cycled back every decade or so for the next three centuries.

events.title: People's Republic of China Proclaimed
events.blurb: Standing above a vast plaza in the Chinese capital, a revolutionary leader announced the founding of a new communist state after two decades of civil war and foreign occupation. His defeated nationalist rival retreated to an island 160 kilometres off the mainland coast and established a rival regime that persists today.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1949 — Mao Zedong declared the PRC from the Tiananmen gate. Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan with 2 million refugees and most of the mainland's gold reserves. The split still defines East Asian geopolitics.

events.title: Suez Crisis
events.blurb: Britain, France, and Israel invaded Egypt to seize the nationalized waterway linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The military operation succeeded; the political one did not. Under combined U.S. and Soviet pressure, the invaders withdrew within two months. The affair is remembered as the moment Britain stopped being a great power.
events.revealBlurb: October 29 to November 7, 1956 — Eisenhower was furious he hadn't been consulted and threatened to sell US holdings of British sterling. British PM Anthony Eden resigned in disgrace three months later. Nasser emerged as the hero of the Arab world.

events.title: Romanian Revolution
events.blurb: Within ten days, a dictator who had ruled a Balkan nation for 24 years lost control of a mass demonstration, fled the capital by helicopter, was captured, given a two-hour military tribunal, and executed by firing squad on Christmas Day alongside his wife. It was the only violent collapse among the eastern bloc regimes that fell at the time.
events.revealBlurb: December 16-25, 1989 — Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu. Soldiers actually had to be ordered to stop shooting them — they kept firing at the already-dead bodies. Ceaușescu's final request was to sing the Internationale. It was denied.

events.title: German Reunification
events.blurb: On a crisp autumn evening, a huge black, red, and gold flag was raised in front of the Reichstag building as the East German state ceased to exist and its 16 million citizens became part of the unified federal republic. Forty-five years of partition, imposed by four occupying armies, ended at the stroke of midnight. Crowds sang the national anthem for the first time as one country.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1990 — the date is now German Unity Day. The integration cost West Germany over €2 trillion over three decades. Many eastern cities still empty out; many western taxpayers still grumble about the "solidarity surcharge."

events.title: August Coup Against Gorbachev
events.blurb: A committee of Soviet hardliners — the KGB chief, the defense minister, the vice president — placed the reform-minded Soviet leader under house arrest at his Black Sea dacha and announced on state television that he was "unwell." Three days of confusion followed. A reformist Russian president climbed atop a tank outside his parliament and defied the plotters. The coup collapsed in 60 hours, and so, effectively, did the union.
events.revealBlurb: August 19-21, 1991 — the tank-top defier was Boris Yeltsin. Gorbachev returned to Moscow to find his authority gutted; Yeltsin had eclipsed him. Within four months the USSR itself would be gone.

events.title: Compact Disc Launches
events.blurb: Sony and Philips released the Compact Disc — a 12-cm polycarbonate-and-aluminum disc encoding digital audio that could be read by a laser — along with the first commercially available CD players. The digital format eventually killed off the vinyl LP and the cassette, promising perfect sound quality and indestructibility (neither claim quite held up). The first commercial CD, launched in Japan, was Billy Joel's "52nd Street."
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1982 — Sony, Philips launch the Compact Disc in Japan. European/US launch March 1983. The 74-minute maximum runtime was reportedly chosen to fit Beethoven's 9th Symphony. Over 200 billion CDs have been manufactured.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: O.J. Simpson Verdict
events.blurb: A Los Angeles Superior Court jury, deliberating for only four hours after eleven months of testimony, found a former NFL running back and actor not guilty of the murders of his ex-wife and her friend. The verdict, announced at 10 AM Pacific time, was watched by an estimated 100 million Americans. National productivity visibly dropped during the broadcast. The decision split along racial lines: most white Americans believed him guilty; most Black Americans were skeptical of the Los Angeles police who had arrested him.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1995 — O.J. Simpson acquitted. Defense lawyers Johnnie Cochran ("If it doesn't fit, you must acquit") and Robert Shapiro. Simpson was later found liable for the deaths in a 1997 civil trial and ordered to pay $33.5 million. He died of cancer in April 2024 at 76.

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: First Spacewalk
events.blurb: Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov floated outside Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock and spent 12 minutes and 9 seconds in open space — the first human extravehicular activity. His spacesuit then ballooned in the vacuum to the point where he could no longer fit back through the hatch, forcing him to bleed pressure from a valve before squeezing inside headfirst.
events.revealBlurb: March 18, 1965 — Voskhod 2. The suit's engineers had fitted it with a built-in suicide pill. Leonov later said sweat filled his boots to the knee from the exertion of forcing himself back in. The spacecraft also drifted into an unplanned orbit and landed 386 km off target in the Ural mountains, where the crew spent a night in wolf country.

events.title: Viking 1 First Mars Landing
events.blurb: NASA's Viking 1 lander touched down on Chryse Planitia, becoming the first spacecraft to successfully land on Mars and operate on its surface. Within minutes it returned the first color photographs of the Martian surface and began a biology experiment suite designed to detect signs of microbial life — whose results remain contested among planetary scientists.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1976 — Viking 1. The landing date was chosen deliberately: it was the seventh anniversary of the Apollo 11 Moon landing. Viking 1 operated for 2,245 Martian days — more than six Earth years — before its final transmission. One biology experiment produced an initially positive result for life that NASA later attributed to reactive soil chemistry.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Curiosity Mars Rover Landing
events.blurb: NASA's Curiosity rover descended through the Martian atmosphere using a novel sky-crane system that lowered the 899 kg rover on nylon cables from a hovering rocket-powered platform before flying away and crashing at a safe distance. The rover landed in Gale Crater and confirmed within the first year that Mars once had liquid water capable of supporting microbial life.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 2012 — Mars Science Laboratory. Engineers called the entry sequence "seven minutes of terror" because Mars is 14 light-minutes away — by the time Earth received confirmation that the descent had begun, Curiosity was already alive or dead on the surface. The first wheel tracks Curiosity made on Mars spelled "JPL" in Morse code.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: Kismet Released
events.blurb: A Bombay Talkies crime film with an unambiguous anti-hero — the lead character is a thief and a cad — opened in the depths of winter during a bitter internal dispute that was tearing the studio apart, yet became the first film in Indian cinema history to gross ₹1 crore. At a Calcutta cinema it ran for 187 consecutive weeks, a record that stood for 32 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 1943, Bombay. Directed by Gyan Mukherjee, starring Ashok Kumar. Its patriotic song "Door Hato Ae Duniyawalon" — aimed at colonial occupation without naming it — spread through cities as independence agitation intensified. The British censors initially approved it without grasping the subtext.

events.title: First National Film Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: India's first government-adjudicated film awards were presented at Vigyan Bhavan in New Delhi by the President of the Republic, honouring the best films of 1953 across features, documentaries, and children's cinema. The ceremony established that Indian cinema was not merely entertainment but a matter of national cultural policy — a position that has shaped every film ministry since.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 1954. First Best Feature Film: Shyamchi Aai, a Marathi film about maternal devotion — not a Bombay product, a signal about the awards' intent to honour all Indian languages. The ceremony was conceived explicitly to reward what the state considered the right kind of cinema.

events.title: Mughal-e-Azam Released
events.blurb: A Mughal-court epic that took sixteen years to complete — halted twice by financial collapse and partitioned away from its original cast — cost ₹1.5 crore, more than any previous Indian film, and spent ₹1 crore on a single song filmed in a replica of the Sheesh Mahal built with imported Belgian glass. Released in black and white, it was the highest-grossing Indian film for fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1960 — directed by K. Asif. The original Akbar died before filming could restart; the entire cast was rebuilt after Partition. In 2004 it became the first Indian black-and-white film to be digitally colourised and theatrically re-released — and was a commercial success all over again.

events.title: Bobby Released
events.blurb: A teen romance between a rich Hindu boy and a poor Goan Christian fisherman's daughter — directed by a father launching his second son into stardom — upended Bollywood's existing template of adult romances and star-crossed melodrama. The film's bikini-clad poster and youth-coded aesthetics signalled an entirely new demographic that filmmakers had been ignoring.
events.revealBlurb: September 29, 1973 — Raj Kapoor directing Rishi Kapoor in his leading-role debut, opposite Dimple Kapadia in hers. The film became the highest-grossing of 1973. Raj Kapoor cast Dimple Kapadia after seeing her at a party; she was sixteen. She married Rajesh Khanna five months after filming wrapped.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Munich Olympics Massacre
events.blurb: Eight armed members of a Palestinian militant group scaled the perimeter fence of an Olympic Village at a German Summer Games, broke into the Israeli team's dormitory apartments, killed two Israeli athletes on the spot, and took nine others hostage. An inept German rescue operation at the military airfield where the hostages and captors had been flown ended with all nine hostages dead along with five of the eight attackers and one German police officer. The Games were suspended for a day, then resumed; the IOC president said that "the Games must go on."
events.revealBlurb: September 5-6, 1972 — Black September. IOC president: Avery Brundage. Israel's government launched a covert years-long assassination campaign against the attack's planners, known as Operation Wrath of God and dramatized in Spielberg's Munich (2005).

events.title: Michael Jordan's First Retirement
events.blurb: Three months after winning his third straight NBA championship and four months after his father had been murdered in a highway robbery, the 30-year-old best basketball player in the world held a press conference announcing his retirement from the game. He had "lost the desire to play," he said. Months later he was playing minor-league baseball for a Chicago White Sox affiliate. He would return to the NBA 17 months after his retirement, winning three more championships.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1993 — Michael Jordan. His AA baseball season with the Birmingham Barons ended with a .202 batting average. His return to the NBA, announced March 18, 1995 with the two-word press release "I'm back," drew him to four more championships (1996, 1997, 1998) before a second retirement, then a third comeback with the Washington Wizards.

events.title: Tiger Woods Wins First Masters
events.blurb: A 21-year-old American golfer, playing in his first Masters as a professional, won the prestigious Augusta tournament by 12 strokes — the largest margin in the event's history — with a record-setting 18-under-par total. He was the youngest winner of a Masters, the first with African ancestry, and the first of Asian heritage. The club had admitted its first Black member only seven years earlier. Viewership had doubled the previous year's; his arrival reshaped the demographics, marketing, and money of professional golf.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1997 — Tiger Woods at Augusta National. He would win 15 major championships across a career including three more Masters wins. His dominance of the sport from 1997 through 2008 has been widely called one of the most influential individual runs in professional sports.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: A Trip to the Moon Released
events.blurb: A former stage magician released a 14-minute narrative film depicting a group of astronomers launched to the Moon in a giant bullet fired from a cannon, encountering hostile selenites, and returning to Earth. Its hand-tinted prints included the most recognizable image in early cinema: a cartoon Moon with a bullet lodged in its eye. It was pirated within months by Thomas Edison's company, which sold copies without paying royalties.
events.revealBlurb: 1902 — Georges Méliès, whose production company Star Film went bankrupt partly from lost piracy revenue. He destroyed many of his own negatives in bitterness; the hand-coloured version was rediscovered in Barcelona in 1993, disintegrating, and painstakingly restored.

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: Fellini's 8½ Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a semi-autobiographical film about a filmmaker suffering a creative block while preparing his next picture, in which the director's own memories, dreams, and erotic fantasies dissolve into the plot he is trying to construct. The Italian title referred literally to the number of films the director had made. It won two Oscars and became the classic film-about-film-making, endlessly quoted by later directors similarly stuck.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 1963 — Federico Fellini, with Marcello Mastroianni as his alter ego. Fellini had genuinely been blocked after a string of successes; the film emerged from trying to work out why. It was remade as a Broadway musical ("Nine") in 1982.

events.title: Pulp Fiction Released
events.blurb: A 31-year-old American director released a 154-minute crime picture with a deliberately non-linear structure, three loosely interwoven storylines, and dialogue about hamburgers, foot massages, and divine intervention. It had cost $8 million, been passed on by multiple studios, and been rescued by a new boutique distributor. It won the top prize at Cannes, grossed over $200 million, and pulled a whole generation of independent filmmakers into its wake.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1994 — Quentin Tarantino, released by Miramax. The opening Cannes screening received a 15-minute standing ovation. John Travolta's comeback, the soundtrack's surf-rock revival, and the dance scene became instant cultural touchstones.

events.title: Titanic Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director released a 195-minute romantic epic about a fictional couple aboard the 1912 maiden voyage of the British ocean liner. The production had been the most expensive in Hollywood history, its budget having doubled during filming; industry wags predicted financial disaster. The film ran in theatres for ten months, won 11 Oscars, and became the first film to gross over a billion dollars. Its director famously shouted "I'm king of the world" from the podium.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1997 — James Cameron, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. It grossed $2.2 billion; Cameron's subsequent "Avatar" beat it 12 years later, also directed by him. Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" spent three weeks at #1.

events.title: Great Chicago Fire
events.blurb: A fire started in a barn on a windy autumn evening in the second-largest U.S. metropolis and burned for 27 hours, destroying 17,500 buildings across 8.5 square kilometres of the central business district and killing around 300 people. A third of the city's population was left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: October 8-10, 1871 — Chicago. The Mrs. O'Leary's cow story is almost certainly a fabrication invented by a reporter who later confessed. On the very same day, the deadlier Peshtigo fire in Wisconsin killed 1,500+ people but is largely forgotten.

events.title: Johnstown Flood
events.blurb: After days of heavy rain, a poorly maintained earth dam built to create a private lake for a Pennsylvania hunting club gave way, releasing 20 million tons of water onto the steel-mill town 23 kilometres downstream. The wall of water reached speeds of 65 km/h and was 18 metres high. It killed 2,209 people in 10 minutes.
events.revealBlurb: May 31, 1889 — Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The hunting club's members (including Andrew Carnegie and Henry Clay Frick) were never successfully sued. The flood launched the American Red Cross onto the national stage; Clara Barton ran relief operations for five months.

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: European Heat Wave
events.blurb: A prolonged period of extreme heat, with temperatures over 40°C across much of western Europe, killed an estimated 70,000 people, mostly elderly apartment-dwellers in cities poorly equipped for such conditions. France alone lost 15,000 lives. Morgues ran out of space; refrigerated trucks were requisitioned.
events.revealBlurb: August 2003 — France, Italy, Spain, UK, and Germany hit hardest. Paris reached 40°C. Many elderly victims were discovered by returning holidaymakers weeks later. France rewrote its social services to check on isolated seniors; subsequent heat waves in 2006, 2019, and 2022 killed far fewer.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Indian National Congress Founded
events.blurb: Seventy-two delegates — mostly English-educated Indian lawyers, journalists, and teachers, along with a few sympathetic Britons — met at a college in a western Indian port city for a three-day conference to petition the colonial government for greater Indian representation in its administration. The polite gathering would, over six decades, become the vehicle of a mass independence movement.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1885 — Bombay (now Mumbai). The prime mover was a retired British civil servant, Allan Octavian Hume, who believed organized political expression would prevent revolution. He was half right.

events.title: Partition of Bengal
events.blurb: A British viceroy, citing administrative efficiency, split a vast eastern province of colonial India into two along religious lines — a Muslim-majority east and a Hindu-majority west — over the fierce protests of its Bengali elite. Boycotts of British goods, the Swadeshi movement, and targeted assassinations followed. The partition was reversed six years later, but the communal logic it had introduced could not be uninvented.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1905 — announced by Lord Curzon. Rabindranath Tagore led Hindus and Muslims in tying rakhis on each other's wrists in protest. The reunification in 1911 coincided with moving the colonial capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Right to Information Act
events.blurb: A law guaranteeing any citizen of the country the right to request information from public authorities — and compelling officials to respond within 30 days or face personal penalties — came into force after a decade-long campaign driven by rural social movements in a western state. It quickly became one of the most-used such laws in the world, exposing corruption from village panchayats to the prime minister's office.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 2005 — RTI Act. Aruna Roy's Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan was the movement's backbone. Its origins lay in drought-era sit-ins demanding to see the village wage registers. More than a hundred RTI activists have been murdered since passage.

events.title: 26/11 Mumbai Attacks
events.blurb: Ten men trained by a Pakistan-based militant group landed at a fishing harbour in the country's financial capital by rubber dinghy after hijacking an Indian fishing trawler at sea, and fanned out across the city to attack a railway station, a Jewish centre, a café, and two luxury hotels. The resulting sieges lasted 60 hours. 166 people died and more than 300 were wounded. Nine attackers were killed; the sole survivor was captured, tried, and hanged four years later.
events.revealBlurb: November 26-29, 2008 — Mumbai. The captured gunman, Ajmal Kasab, was hanged on November 21, 2012. The attacks were coordinated over satellite phone from Karachi; the operational planner, Sajid Mir, was finally convicted in Pakistan in 2022.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Benazir Bhutto Becomes PM
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Oxford and Harvard educated politician whose father had been hanged by a previous military government was sworn in as prime minister of a large South Asian Muslim-majority country, becoming the first woman to head the government of any Muslim-majority state. Her ruling coalition was fragile; she would be dismissed twice on corruption charges and would be assassinated 19 years later while campaigning for a third term.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1988 — Benazir Bhutto of Pakistan. She was assassinated in Rawalpindi on December 27, 2007, after a campaign rally. Her 19-year-old son Bilawal was named co-chair of her party within days.

events.title: Angela Merkel Becomes Chancellor
events.blurb: A physicist from a former communist state in central Europe, who had entered politics only after the collapse of her country's ruling party, was sworn in as the first woman head of a reunified German government. She would hold the office for 16 years through four terms, becoming the effective leader of Europe during the eurozone debt crisis, the Syrian refugee crisis, and the first waves of the COVID-19 pandemic.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 2005 — Angela Merkel of the CDU. She retired voluntarily in December 2021, the first German chancellor in 70 years to do so. She had become known as "Mutti" (Mommy) — half-affectionate, half-exasperated.

events.title: Malala Yousafzai Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Pakistani girl, who had been shot in the head by a Taliban gunman on her school bus two years earlier for publicly advocating for girls' education, became the youngest-ever winner of the world's most prestigious peace prize. She shared the award with an Indian child-rights activist. She had been giving anonymous interviews to the BBC since age 11; she was now a household name.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 2014 — Malala Yousafzai and Kailash Satyarthi. She was attacked on October 9, 2012 in Swat Valley and underwent multiple surgeries in the UK. Her autobiography had been published the previous year. She was 11 years below the previous youngest laureate.

events.title: #MeToo Goes Viral
events.blurb: Five days after a major U.S. newspaper published a long investigation into sexual harassment and assault allegations against a powerful Hollywood film producer, an actress posted on Twitter asking women who had been sexually harassed or assaulted to reply with two words. Within 24 hours, those two words had been used 500,000 times on Twitter alone. The phrase had been coined a decade earlier by a Black activist working with survivors in the American South.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2017 — Alyssa Milano's tweet; the phrase was coined in 2006 by Tarana Burke. The producer was Harvey Weinstein, finally convicted of rape in February 2020. A cascade of resignations, prosecutions, and cultural reckoning followed across industries.

events.title: One Thousand and One Nights Compiled
events.blurb: An anonymous Arabic compiler assembled a frame narrative and embedded stories drawn from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian, and Egyptian sources into a single cycle. The outer frame told of a queen stalling her own execution by telling her king a new story every night; the inner tales — of flying carpets, genies, thieves — became permanent fixtures of world storytelling. The collection continued to accrete new tales for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 10th century CE — the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript dates from the 14th century. "Aladdin," "Ali Baba," and "Sinbad" were added to the collection by an 18th-century French translator, Antoine Galland, working from Syrian oral sources. They are not in the original Arabic canon.

events.title: Moby-Dick Published
events.blurb: A 31-year-old American novelist published his sixth novel — a 135-chapter whaling yarn interleaved with encyclopedic digressions on cetacean anatomy, metaphysical speculation, and a revenge monomania culminating in an apocalyptic confrontation with a great white whale. The book sold 3,215 copies in its first 18 months and then essentially nothing for decades. The author died largely forgotten. The rediscovery of the novel's greatness did not come until the 1920s.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1851 — Herman Melville. The white whale was loosely based on a real albino sperm whale, Mocha Dick, which reportedly stove in ships. The book was first published in London as "The Whale"; the American edition restored the title "Moby-Dick; or, The Whale."

events.title: Walden Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Massachusetts essayist, graduate of Harvard, former schoolteacher, and occasional pencil-factory worker, published an account of two years and two months he had spent living in a cabin he had built himself beside a glacier-pond near Concord. The book mixed natural observation, economic criticism, and philosophical reflection. It sold slowly; its reputation grew after the author's early death seven years later, and he is now considered one of the founders of American nature writing.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1854 — Henry David Thoreau. He had lived at Walden Pond 1845-47. The pond was, contrary to legend, a short walk from his family home; his mother did his laundry. Thoreau's civil-disobedience essay would later inspire Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

events.title: Things Fall Apart Published
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Nigerian broadcaster published a short novel tracing the life of an Igbo wrestler and farmer in a southeastern Nigerian village and the arrival of English colonial missionaries that destroys his world. Written in English deliberately infused with Igbo idiom, the book pushed back against European literary stereotypes of African societies. It has since been translated into 50 languages and sold over 20 million copies — the most widely read book by any African author.
events.revealBlurb: 1958 — Chinua Achebe. Its title is from Yeats's poem "The Second Coming." Achebe later famously accused Joseph Conrad of racism in "Heart of Darkness." He was in a serious car crash in 1990 that left him paralyzed from the waist down; he continued writing for over two more decades.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Columbus Reaches the Americas
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator captaining three small Spanish ships, after 33 days of open-Atlantic sailing from the Canary Islands with an increasingly mutinous crew, sighted land just after 2 AM — a low-lying island he promptly named after a Christian saviour. He was convinced, and would die still convinced, that he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The four voyages he made over the next twelve years reshaped two continents.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 1492 — Christopher Columbus made landfall on Guanahani in the Bahamas. The lookout who first sighted land, Rodrigo de Triana, did not receive the promised reward — Columbus claimed he had seen a light the previous evening. The contact collapsed Indigenous populations via epidemic disease within decades.

events.title: Fall of Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: After a three-month siege — during which Spanish-allied Indigenous forces demolished the city district by district, channeled the causeways, and introduced a devastating smallpox epidemic — the last Aztec emperor surrendered in a canoe on the lake as his capital burned. The Spaniards, led by Cortés, renamed the ruins and built a viceregal capital on them. The Aztec empire ceased to exist; the Spanish conquest of the Americas was underway.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1521 — Cuauhtémoc surrendered to Cortés. The city's population had dropped from perhaps 200,000 to under 50,000 through disease, siege starvation, and fighting. The Spanish built Mexico City on the drained lakebed — which continues to sink today at 50 cm per year.

events.title: Elizabeth I Accession
events.blurb: A 25-year-old unmarried princess, the daughter of a beheaded second queen who had once been declared a bastard, became Queen of England on the death of her half-sister. She had survived imprisonment and political marginalization under her sister's Catholic restoration. Her 44-year reign would see the English settlement of Ireland, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flowering of Shakespeare, and the establishment of a Protestant national church still in existence.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1558 — Elizabeth I Tudor succeeds Mary I. She reportedly received the news sitting under an oak tree at Hatfield House. She never married, styled herself the "Virgin Queen," and died at 69. The state of Virginia — briefly colonized under her — is named for her.

events.title: Mayflower Compact Signed
events.blurb: 41 male passengers of a merchant ship that had landed at the wrong spot on the Massachusetts coast — they had intended the Hudson River — signed a short agreement on the ship to govern themselves by the will of the majority until permanent civil authority could be established. The document was pragmatic, not ideological, but became a foundational text of American self-government. The Pilgrims who signed it were fleeing religious persecution in England via the Netherlands.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 1620 (Old Style) / November 21, 1620 (New Style) — aboard the Mayflower, Cape Cod. Half the colony's 102 passengers died of scurvy and starvation the first winter. The autumn 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag is the ancestor of the American Thanksgiving.

events.title: Bacon's Novum Organum
events.blurb: A 59-year-old English Lord Chancellor published a Latin treatise proposing a new method for the natural sciences — not the deduction from first principles that Aristotelian scholars had relied on for eighteen centuries, but the patient inductive accumulation of observations, cataloguing of anomalies, and testing of hypotheses. The method he described, refined and formalized over the next century, became recognizable as the modern scientific method.
events.revealBlurb: 1620 — Francis Bacon, "Novum Organum Scientiarum." He was dismissed from the Lord Chancellorship the next year for taking bribes. He died in 1626 after catching pneumonia from stuffing a chicken with snow to study the preservation of meat — an early experimental death.

events.title: Boston Tea Party
events.blurb: That winter night, some 116 colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, destroying approximately £10,000 worth of merchandise. The targeted destruction was a direct protest against the Tea Act, which granted the company a monopoly while taxing colonial consumers.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1773 — Boston Harbor. Not a single participant was ever prosecuted. Britain's furious response — the Coercive Acts, which colonists renamed the Intolerable Acts — did more to unify colonial resistance than the tea party itself. The name "Boston Tea Party" wasn't coined until decades later.

events.title: British Surrender at Saratoga
events.blurb: A British army of 6,000 men under a genteel general who had marched south from Canada intending to split the American colonies along the Hudson Valley found itself encircled at a rural New York hamlet after two pitched battles and dwindling supplies. The general surrendered his entire force to the American commander. It was the most consequential Allied success of the war; France, which had been secretly aiding the colonies, publicly entered the conflict four months later.
events.revealBlurb: October 17, 1777 — British general John Burgoyne surrenders to American general Horatio Gates. Burgoyne had been marching from Canada; a complementary British push up the Hudson from New York had been misdirected to Pennsylvania. The victory secured French diplomatic recognition and military alliance.

events.title: Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown
events.blurb: A British army of 8,000 men under a peer of the realm, trapped on a Virginia peninsula by a combined Franco-American land force and blocked from the Chesapeake by a French fleet, surrendered after a three-week siege. The British commander, reportedly feigning illness, sent a deputy to the surrender ceremony; his band played a tune called "The World Turned Upside Down." The war dragged on in minor engagements for two more years but the outcome was no longer in doubt.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 1781 — Lord Cornwallis surrenders to General George Washington and Comte de Rochambeau at Yorktown, Virginia. The French navy's blockade, commanded by Admiral de Grasse, decided the siege. Formal peace negotiations began within months.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Haiti Declares Independence
events.blurb: A former slave turned general, addressing a small crowd at a town on a Caribbean island, declared the independence of a new sovereign state that replaced a French sugar colony. It took the name of the original Taíno indigenous word for the island. It was the first independent state in Latin America, the only one to emerge from a successful slave revolt, and the second republic in the Western hemisphere. European powers reacted with diplomatic ostracism; the United States refused recognition for 58 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1804 — Jean-Jacques Dessalines at Gonaïves, Haiti. France demanded reparations for "lost property" — 150 million francs — that Haiti finished paying only in 1947. The combination of debt, ostracism, and internal strife has shaped Haitian poverty for two centuries.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.blurb: A Norman duke from across the English Channel invaded a southern English kingdom with 7,000 men, met its exhausted king — who had marched south after defeating a Norwegian invasion three weeks earlier in the north — on a hillside near the coast, and won in an all-day battle. The English king was killed, reportedly by an arrow through the eye. The victor replaced the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy with his own.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1066 — William the Conqueror vs. Harold Godwinson near the town of Battle, East Sussex. The Bayeux Tapestry, a 70-metre embroidered account, was sewn within a decade. Modern English is still 50–60 percent French-derived because of the resulting Norman elite.

events.title: Peasants' Revolt
events.blurb: A rebellion over a hated poll tax swept through southeast England, with rural peasants and urban artisans marching on the capital, burning a palace and a law library, and executing the royal treasurer and the archbishop on the spot. The 14-year-old king met the rebels in person twice; the second meeting ended when the mayor stabbed their leader on the royal's behalf. Reprisals followed.
events.revealBlurb: May to November 1381 — Wat Tyler killed at Smithfield on June 15. Richard II, 14, rode forward after Tyler fell and said: "You will have no captain but me." The rebels went home; the king's negotiated concessions were rescinded within weeks.

events.title: Battle of Agincourt
events.blurb: An exhausted English army, heavily outnumbered, caught in thick mud on a narrow front between two woods in northern France, stood behind sharpened wooden stakes and cut down the armored flower of French nobility with longbows at point-blank range. The French dead included a constable, three dukes, and over 1,500 knights; English losses were perhaps 400. Shakespeare would turn it into a speech 180 years later.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1415 — Henry V on St. Crispin's Day. Henry ordered the slaughter of prisoners mid-battle when he feared a rear attack; this remains controversial. The longbow's armor-piercing arrowheads were called "bodkins."

events.title: Siege of Orléans Lifted
events.blurb: A 17-year-old peasant girl from Lorraine, dressed in white armour and claiming visions from saints, led a French relief army into a besieged Loire Valley city. Over eight days of sorties, she personally led assaults on the English siege forts around the city, was shot through the shoulder with a crossbow bolt, returned to the fight, and broke the siege. The French war effort, exhausted for a generation, was transformed overnight.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1429 — Joan of Arc relieves Orléans. She had convinced a skeptical Dauphin to give her an army by passing a theological interrogation and, reportedly, a virginity test. She would see him crowned as Charles VII at Reims within ten weeks.

events.title: First Punic War Begins
events.blurb: The Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire, the two rising powers of the western Mediterranean, went to war over control of a large island between them. The conflict would last 23 years and transform Rome from a purely land-based power into a naval one — the Romans, ignorant of shipbuilding, reportedly reverse-engineered a captured Carthaginian warship to build their first fleet. Rome eventually won and imposed a crushing indemnity; the seed of two more wars was planted.
events.revealBlurb: 264 BCE — Rome vs. Carthage over Sicily. "Punic" comes from the Latin for "Phoenician," Carthage's origin. The Romans invented boarding bridges ("corvi") that turned sea battles into quasi-land battles they could win. Rome lost 700 ships over the course of the war, mostly to storms.

events.title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Carthaginian general marched an army of 50,000 men, 9,000 cavalry, and 37 war elephants from Iberia over the Alps into northern Italy over 15 days of early winter, intending to take the war to Rome's home territory. Half his men died in the crossing from cold, hunger, and hostile Alpine tribes. The force that did make it to Italy shocked Rome by winning three successive battles within two years, annihilating Roman legions at Trebbia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae.
events.revealBlurb: 218 BCE — Hannibal Barca. The exact Alpine pass he used is still debated; the leading candidates are the Col de la Traversette or the Col du Mont Cenis. Only a few elephants made it across and most died in Italy's wet winter. Hannibal won tactically but could not take Rome itself.

events.title: Julius Caesar Assassinated
events.blurb: A Roman dictator, having been named dictator-for-life a month earlier, was stabbed 23 times by a group of 60 senators at a meeting of the Senate held in a Pompey-built theatre. The assassins, styling themselves "Liberators," had convinced themselves that removing the man who had effectively ended the Republic would restore it. Instead, his death plunged Rome into 14 more years of civil war, at the end of which his adopted heir emerged as the first Roman emperor in all but name.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 44 BCE — the Ides of March. Conspirators included Brutus and Cassius. The supposed last words "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare; Caesar's actual last words — if he spoke any — may have been the Greek "kai su, teknon?" ("you too, my child?"). His heir Octavian defeated the conspirators at Philippi two years later.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.blurb: After Rome settled Visigothic refugees south of the Danube and then systematically starved and abused them, the Goths rose in revolt. Emperor Valens — who refused to wait for reinforcements — attacked their fortified camp with approximately 30,000 men. Gothic cavalry flanked both sides of the Roman line and trapped the legions; two-thirds of the eastern field army was destroyed and Valens himself was killed.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 378 CE. Valens's body was never found. One account says he was carried wounded to a farmhouse, which Gothic soldiers then set alight; another says he was lost in the general slaughter. Military historians sometimes call Adrianople "the ancient world's Stalingrad."

events.title: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
events.blurb: A Visigothic king and his army, frustrated by failed negotiations with a Western Roman emperor for lands and subsidies, entered Rome itself through an unguarded gate and spent three days pillaging. It was the first time the city had been sacked since the Gauls in 390 BCE — eight centuries earlier. The city's wealth and status had made it symbolically untouchable; the shock rippled through the Mediterranean world. Pagans blamed Rome's adoption of Christianity; Augustine wrote "The City of God" partly in response.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 410 CE — Alaric I the Visigoth. The emperor Honorius was safely in Ravenna, the western capital since 402. The historian Jerome wrote from Bethlehem: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken." Alaric died of illness a few months after the sack.

events.title: Intel 4004 Microprocessor Released
events.blurb: Intel released a 4-bit central processing unit containing 2,300 transistors on a silicon chip the size of a fingernail, capable of 60,000 operations per second. Originally designed for a Japanese calculator company, it became the world's first commercially available microprocessor — the prototype for every CPU that followed.

events.title: Intel 4004 Released
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley chipmaker released the first commercial microprocessor — a single integrated circuit 3 millimetres long containing 2,300 transistors, clocking at 740 kilohertz, capable of computing roughly as fast as the 30-tonne ENIAC 25 years earlier. It had been developed as a calculator chip for a Japanese customer. Its designers convinced Intel's management to retain the design rights and market it as a general-purpose product.
events.revealBlurb: November 15, 1971 — Intel 4004. Designers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. The 4-bit chip cost $200. Intel's 1971 product-line predecessor was the 3101 memory chip; it now sells trillions of transistors per year.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Forbidden City Completed
events.blurb: A Ming-dynasty emperor completed an imperial palace complex at the center of his new northern capital — 980 buildings, 9,999 rooms, on a site of 72 hectares, enclosed by a moat and a 10-metre wall. It served as the home and ceremonial centre of 24 successive emperors across two dynasties. The compound was closed to the public for 500 years; it was opened as a museum after the abdication of the last Qing emperor in 1912.
events.revealBlurb: 1420 — the Yongle Emperor, completing the move of the Ming capital from Nanjing to Beijing. Over a million workers built it in 14 years. The last emperor to live there was Puyi, who was expelled in 1924. It is now China's most-visited museum.

events.title: Statue of Liberty Dedicated
events.blurb: A 46-metre-tall copper statue of a robed woman holding a torch, a gift from the French people commemorating American independence (with an eye toward French republican aspirations), was dedicated on a small island in New York Harbor in the rain. It had been designed by a French sculptor, its internal iron framework engineered by the man who would five years later design a certain Paris tower, and shipped across the Atlantic in 350 pieces.
events.revealBlurb: October 28, 1886 — sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi; engineer Gustave Eiffel. The statue was meant to arrive for the 1876 centennial; it missed by a decade due to fundraising troubles. The poem on its pedestal ("Give me your tired, your poor...") was added in 1903 from a sonnet by Emma Lazarus.

events.title: Hoover Dam Completed
events.blurb: A 221-metre concrete arch-gravity dam across the Colorado River at a deep canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border was completed two years ahead of schedule, creating what was at the time the largest reservoir on the planet. The dam's construction employed 16,000 workers during the worst years of the Great Depression; 96 died during the 5-year project. It generated 2,080 megawatts, ran every light in Las Vegas, irrigated a million acres, and made the Los Angeles basin's growth possible.
events.revealBlurb: September 30, 1935 — originally called the Boulder Dam under Roosevelt's administration; renamed 1947 after Herbert Hoover, who had championed the project as Commerce Secretary. Around 6 million tons of concrete went into it — enough, with less, to pave a two-lane road from San Francisco to New York.

events.title: Sydney Opera House Opens
events.blurb: A sail-shaped performing-arts complex on a harbour peninsula opened after 14 years of construction — ten times its original budget and nine years late. The Danish architect had won the design competition in 1957 but resigned in 1966 after political attacks and budget fights; he never saw the completed building. Its concrete "sails," covered in a million tiles of two shades of white, immediately made it one of the most recognized buildings in the world.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1973 — architect Jørn Utzon; opened by Queen Elizabeth II. Utzon was eventually reconciled with the building in 1999, 25 years after he left; he was awarded the Pritzker Prize in 2003 but never saw the interior of his own building. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: A constitutional amendment prohibiting the denial of voting rights "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude" was ratified, giving Black men the theoretical right to vote. Within three decades, poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and organized terror had effectively erased Black voting across the former Confederacy.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1870. It took the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — 95 years later — to make the amendment's promise practical. Black women were excluded not by race but by sex until the 19th Amendment in 1920.

events.title: Military Desegregation Order
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed an executive order mandating "equality of treatment and opportunity" in the armed forces without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. The army resisted for nearly five years; full integration of combat units was not achieved until the Korean War made ignoring Black replacements impossible.
events.revealBlurb: July 26, 1948 — Executive Order 9981, Harry Truman. He signed it partly out of conviction, partly because Black voters in northern cities were now pivotal to Democratic victory. The last all-Black unit was dissolved in 1954.

events.title: Malcolm X Assassinated
events.blurb: A charismatic Black Muslim minister who had broken with the Nation of Islam a year earlier was shot 21 times by three gunmen as he rose to address an audience at a Harlem ballroom. He was 39. The three men convicted of the killing included two who were demonstrably not at the scene; their convictions were overturned in 2021 after a decades-long campaign by their families and a Netflix documentary.
events.revealBlurb: February 21, 1965 — Audubon Ballroom, Manhattan. Malcolm had suffered an assassination attempt at his home a week earlier. His autobiography, co-written with Alex Haley and published posthumously, remains required reading in American universities.

events.title: Black Panther Party Founded
events.blurb: Two community-college students in a California Bay Area city drafted a ten-point program demanding full employment, decent housing, exemption from military service, and an end to police brutality for Black Americans. They organized armed neighborhood patrols to monitor police, opened free-breakfast programs for children, and ran medical clinics. The FBI declared them "the greatest threat to internal security" within four years.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 1966 — Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland. J. Edgar Hoover's COINTELPRO infiltrated the party and fabricated rivalries between it and the US Organization; the free breakfasts, which he called "the greatest threat," fed 20,000 children a day at their peak.

events.title: George Floyd Murdered
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Black man was killed in a Midwestern American city when a white police officer kneeled on his neck for 9 minutes and 29 seconds while he was handcuffed face-down on the pavement. A 17-year-old bystander filmed the entire encounter on her phone. The video triggered the largest protest movement in American history — 15 to 26 million people marched across all 50 states over the following weeks.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 2020 — Minneapolis, officer Derek Chauvin. The bystander was Darnella Frazier; she received a Pulitzer Prize special citation. Chauvin was convicted of second-degree murder 11 months later and sentenced to 22 years. Protests spread to more than 60 countries.

events.title: Battle of Zama
events.blurb: Scipio Africanus neutralised Hannibal's 80 war elephants by opening lanes in his formation so they stampeded harmlessly through, then used superior cavalry to encircle the Carthaginian infantry. Roughly 20,000 Carthaginians died; Carthage accepted a peace stripping it of its fleet, all war elephants, and 10,000 silver talents paid over fifty years.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 202 BCE, North Africa. This was the only time in Hannibal's career that his battle plan failed. After the war, Scipio received the cognomen "Africanus"; his grateful soldiers offered to make him king of Rome, which he refused.

events.title: Sulla's March on Rome
events.blurb: When the Senate transferred his military command to a political rival, consul Lucius Sulla marched six legions across the pomerium — the sacred city boundary no Roman general had ever crossed in arms — and took Rome by force. It was the first time in the Republic's history that a sitting consul used his own army to seize the capital; most of his officers refused the order and resigned rather than obey.
events.revealBlurb: 88 BCE, Rome. After taking the city Sulla had his enemies declared public enemies, then left for his original campaign in Greece as if nothing unusual had happened. His opponent Marius promptly retook Rome, declared Sulla a criminal, and died of old age seven days into his seventh consulship.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.blurb: A group of Roman senators led by Cassius and Brutus surrounded the dictator in the Theatre of Pompey and stabbed him twenty-three times. A later physician concluded only one wound was fatal; the man fell at the base of a statue of his former rival, Pompey himself.
events.revealBlurb: The Ides of March, 44 BCE. Caesar had been warned by a soothsayer to "beware the Ides of March" and laughed it off the same morning. His last words, "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare — ancient sources quote him saying "You too, child?" in Greek.

events.title: Beginning of the Crisis of the Third Century
events.blurb: The assassination of Emperor Severus Alexander by his own troops triggered nearly fifty years of catastrophic instability: more than twenty emperors in half a century, nearly all killed by soldiers or rivals, with simultaneous invasions across every frontier and a fragmenting empire that briefly split into three competing states. The population and economy contracted severely.
events.revealBlurb: 235 CE, Germany. Maximinus Thrax, the soldier who replaced Severus Alexander, was reportedly 8 feet tall and drank a wheelbarrow's worth of water per day — details that are almost certainly exaggerated. He never visited Rome during his three-year reign and was killed by his own troops outside Aquileia.

events.title: Aurelian Reunifies the Empire
events.blurb: After the empire had fractured into three competing states, Emperor Aurelian defeated the Palmyrene Empire in the east — capturing its queen Zenobia — and then the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, bringing Britain, Gaul, Spain, Syria, and Egypt back under a single ruler within five years of taking power. He then began building a massive new defensive wall around Rome itself.
events.revealBlurb: 274 CE. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra had claimed descent from Cleopatra and ruled a sophisticated court of scholars and poets while commanding legions across the Near East. After capture she was eventually settled near Tivoli and, according to some sources, married a Roman senator.

events.title: Mother India Released
events.blurb: A near-three-hour epic about a village woman who spends decades breaking stones, raising sons, and protecting her community from a money-lender opened on Diwali across India and broke every box-office record to that point. The following year it became India's first film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film — losing by a single vote to a Federico Fellini picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1957. Directed by Mehboob Khan. Nargis, who plays the mother, married co-star Sunil Dutt after he dragged her unconscious from a fire that broke out on set. Khan's production logo featured a hammer-and-sickle; it was quietly removed before the Oscar submission print.

events.title: Zanjeer Released
events.blurb: After fifteen consecutive flops, a young actor was offered the role of an angry, incorruptible police inspector in a crime thriller that every major star of the decade — Dharmendra, Dev Anand, Rajesh Khanna — had turned down. The film's success redirected an entire industry's idea of what a Hindi film hero could look like: not romantic or comic, but furious.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1973 — written by Salim-Javed, directed by Prakash Mehra. Amitabh Bachchan was cast almost by elimination. Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar then wrote nearly every subsequent Bachchan blockbuster with him specifically in mind, insisting on his casting as a contractual condition.

events.title: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge Released
events.blurb: A romance about two Non-Resident Indians falling in love on a Eurorail trip before battling parental disapproval opened in Bombay that autumn and never fully left: it ran continuously at one Mumbai cinema for over two decades, setting a record no Indian film has matched. Its climactic train-platform scene became shorthand for every subsequent Bollywood love story.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1995 — Aditya Chopra's directorial debut, age 23. He refused to watch the film with an audience for years. Shah Rukh Khan initially had reservations about the role. The film ran at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir theatre without interruption until 2023 — 1,278 weeks.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: Jawan Released
events.blurb: A Tamil director's Hindi-film debut — a dual-role action thriller mixing vigilante politics with hospital corruption — earned ₹75 crore on its opening day, making it the highest-opening-day gross in Hindi cinema at the time, then crossed ₹600 crore domestically, becoming the first Hindi film to do so. Its release capped a year in which its star reclaimed the top of the industry after a decade's absence.
events.revealBlurb: September 7, 2023 — directed by Atlee. Shah Rukh Khan's return, following Pathaan earlier that year, made 2023 the most commercially dominant single-year performance by any one actor in Bollywood history. The film's opening credits featured cameos by over thirty prominent South Indian actors.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim. Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Homestead Strike
events.blurb: A Pennsylvania steelworkers' strike against wage cuts at a mill owned by a famous industrialist turned into a gun battle after management hired 300 Pinkerton private detectives to escort strike-breakers into the plant. The Pinkertons arrived by barge up the Monongahela River before dawn; strikers and their families met them on the banks with rifles. Nine strikers and seven Pinkertons died in the all-day firefight. The state militia restored order; the union was broken; US steelworkers remained largely non-unionized for 45 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1892 — Homestead Steel Works, owned by Andrew Carnegie, managed during the strike by Henry Clay Frick. Frick survived an assassination attempt by anarchist Alexander Berkman three weeks later, shot and stabbed multiple times but recovered. Carnegie was in Scotland when the violence occurred.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: First Moving Assembly Line
events.blurb: A Detroit automobile company introduced a moving chassis-assembly line at its Highland Park plant, cutting the time needed to assemble a car from 12 hours to 93 minutes. The innovation — borrowed in part from Chicago meatpacking "disassembly" lines — let the company slash prices and dramatically increase production. The line's relentless pace was hated by workers; the company had to double wages the following year to keep them on the job.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1913 — Ford Motor Company, Highland Park plant. The $5/day wage (equivalent to about $140/day today) followed on January 5, 1914. Workers' turnover at the plant dropped from 370 percent annually to near zero. The wage offer drew applicants by the thousands; police had to turn away crowds in a near-riot.

events.title: Hungarian Revolution
events.blurb: A student demonstration in Budapest grew within hours into a nationwide uprising against a Moscow-backed government. For twelve days, a reform-minded premier announced democratic elections and withdrawal from the eastern bloc military alliance. Then 2,500 Soviet tanks rolled into the country, crushing the revolt and killing some 2,500 Hungarians.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 to November 10, 1956 — reform premier Imre Nagy was tricked into a "negotiation," arrested, and secretly executed two years later. 200,000 Hungarians fled west. The West's failure to intervene exposed the limits of containment.

events.title: U-2 Incident
events.blurb: A high-altitude American reconnaissance aircraft was shot down deep inside Soviet territory by a surface-to-air missile.
