The CIA assumed the pilot was dead and issued a cover story about a weather research flight gone astray. Then Khrushchev triumphantly produced the pilot alive and the wreckage intact, humiliating the U.S. president on the eve of a Paris summit.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1960 — pilot Francis Gary Powers ejected over Sverdlovsk (now Yekaterinburg). He was traded two years later for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel on Berlin's Glienicke Bridge — the same swap dramatized in "Bridge of Spies."

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Address
events.blurb: An American president delivered a 17-minute televised address revealing that Soviet nuclear missiles had been discovered on a Caribbean island 145 kilometres from Florida, demanding their removal within a strict deadline. The 13-day standoff that followed was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange, with submarines on both sides carrying armed torpedoes.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis: JFK Announces Naval Blockade
events.blurb: On the 22nd of that month, President John F. Kennedy delivered a nationally televised address revealing that U.S. reconnaissance aircraft had discovered Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba — 90 miles from Florida — and announcing a naval "quarantine" to prevent further weapons deliveries. For 13 days, the United States and Soviet Union stood closer to nuclear war than at any other moment in history before or since.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 1962 — Washington, D.C. Kennedy called it a "quarantine" because a blockade is an act of war under international law. Soviet ships turned around on October 24. The secret resolution involved the U.S. quietly removing its Jupiter missiles from Turkey — a concession Kennedy couldn't publicly acknowledge for decades.

events.title: Helsinki Accords
events.blurb: Thirty-five nations — every European country except tiny Albania, plus the U.S. and Canada — signed a sweeping final act in the Finnish capital that acknowledged post-war borders while binding signatories to respect human rights. Critics called it a sellout to Moscow. In fact, its human rights provisions gave eastern dissidents a legal framework that would undermine the regimes a decade later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1975 — the "Third Basket" on human rights proved subversive. Czech dissidents founded Charter 77 using its language; the Moscow Helsinki Group followed. Brezhnev didn't realize he'd just signed his system's eventual death warrant.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Second Battle of El Alamein
events.blurb: A British commander who had spent three months rebuilding his army launched a night artillery barrage from 1,000 guns and began grinding through minefields and fortified positions across the Egyptian desert, slowly destroying an Axis force that had driven to within 100 kilometres of a strategically critical port city.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 – November 4, 1942. Montgomery's artillery fired 529,000 shells in the opening barrage. Rommel was on sick leave in Austria when the battle opened; Hitler ordered him back by telegram. After twelve days, Rommel began a 2,000-kilometre retreat across North Africa that ended with final Axis surrender in Tunisia six months later.

events.title: First Nuclear Chain Reaction
events.blurb: In a squash court beneath a university stadium, a team of physicists assembled 45,000 carefully machined blocks of graphite around pellets of uranium into a lattice the size of a house, withdrew a control rod, and achieved humanity's first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction — completing the key step toward a new category of weapon.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1942, under Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. Enrico Fermi's team celebrated with a bottle of Chianti in paper cups. The coded telegram sent to Washington read: "The Italian navigator has just landed in the New World." The reactor sat in a populated neighbourhood with no containment vessel.

events.title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.blurb: Over four days, 282 warships clashed in four separate engagements across several hundred thousand square kilometres of open ocean — the largest naval battle in history by tonnage and personnel — as one navy committed virtually everything it had left to stop an invasion and the other deployed over 300 ships to press it through.
events.revealBlurb: October 23–26, 1944. Japan used its remaining fleet carriers as decoys with almost no aircraft aboard. A small force of US destroyers and escort carriers somehow bluffed a vastly superior Japanese battleship force into retreating at the Battle of Samar — one of the most improbable tactical reversals of the war. Japan also deployed kamikaze suicide aircraft in force for the first time.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima
events.blurb: A single aircraft flying at high altitude released a single bomb over a mid-sized city at 8:15 in the morning, detonating it 600 metres above a distinctive T-shaped bridge with the force of 15,000 tons of TNT — flattening 13 square kilometres, killing between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, and ultimately causing 140,000 deaths by the end of the year.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, dropped "Little Boy" over Hiroshima. The aiming point was the Aioi Bridge. The bomb missed by about 250 metres but it did not matter. Tibbets's mother's name was Enola Gay. The co-pilot, Robert Lewis, wrote in his journal: "My God, what have we done?"

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring
events.blurb: A Dutch painter in his early thirties completed an intimate oil study on canvas of a young woman turning toward the viewer, her head covered in a blue and yellow turban, a single teardrop-shaped pearl catching the light at her ear. It was not a commissioned portrait but a "tronie" — a character study. The artist made only about 35 paintings in his career; this one was rediscovered in 1881 at auction for two guilders.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1665 — Johannes Vermeer. Now in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. The "pearl" may actually be tin or glass — no pearl of that size is plausible. Tracy Chevalier's 1999 novel and the 2003 film made it a pop-culture icon.

events.title: First Impressionist Exhibition
events.blurb: Thirty painters whose work had been repeatedly rejected by the official French Salon rented the studio of a photographer on a Paris boulevard and held their own group show. A review in a satirical magazine mocked one of the paintings — "Impression, Sunrise" — and gave the movement the name it would keep. The show attracted 3,500 visitors, which was dismal; mockery outweighed admiration; most of the painters struggled financially for another decade.
events.revealBlurb: April 15 to May 15, 1874 — 35 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris. Participants included Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Cézanne, Berthe Morisot, and Sisley. The critic who coined the term, Louis Leroy, titled his review "Exhibition of the Impressionists" sarcastically; the painters adopted it.

events.title: Armory Show Opens
events.blurb: An exhibition at a New York National Guard armory introduced American audiences to European modernism at industrial scale — 1,300 paintings and sculptures by artists most had never heard of, including Matisse, Picasso, Duchamp, and Brancusi. Duchamp's "Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2" was ridiculed by a popular cartoonist as "explosion in a shingle factory" and drew crowds for exactly that reason. The show moved on to Chicago and Boston and is credited with changing the course of American art.
events.revealBlurb: February 17 to March 15, 1913 — the 69th Regiment Armory, Lexington Avenue, NYC. Around 90,000 people visited in New York alone. Theodore Roosevelt wrote a mostly-baffled review; a reproduction of the "Nude" was burned in effigy at the Chicago Art Institute.

events.title: Kahlo's The Two Fridas
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Mexican painter produced her largest painting — two life-sized self-portraits seated side-by-side on a bench, their hearts exposed and linked by an artery, against a stormy sky. The double figure depicted her divided heritage (her Mexican and European sides) and also the raw aftermath of her divorce from a fellow painter, which had become final three months earlier. She would remarry him a year later.
events.revealBlurb: 1939 — Frida Kahlo, shortly after divorcing Diego Rivera. Now in Mexico City's Museo de Arte Moderno. It was the largest canvas she ever painted, about 1.7 metres square. Kahlo's work reached superstar popularity only decades after her 1954 death.

events.title: First ARPANET Message
events.blurb: A graduate student at a California university tried to log in remotely to a computer at a research institute 560 kilometres north. He typed "L," then "O," then tried to type "G" — and the receiving computer crashed. The first ever message transmitted between two computers on what would grow into the global network was thus the two-letter sequence "lo."
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1969 — UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute. The student was Charley Kline. ARPANET was funded by the Pentagon to enable communication after a nuclear strike. The network went from 4 nodes to 37 in three years.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: Amazon Founded
events.blurb: A former hedge-fund vice-president who had driven across the country from New York to Seattle with his wife, writing a business plan on the way, incorporated an online book retailer in the garage of a rented house in a Seattle suburb. He had chosen books because no single physical store could stock every book in print, but one big warehouse could. The company's first website was clunky; the logic was unstoppable.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1994 — Jeff Bezos. The company was originally called Cadabra; Bezos changed it after a lawyer misheard it as "cadaver." He considered and rejected relentless.com (now redirecting to Amazon).

events.title: Y2K Rollover
events.blurb: As the world's time zones successively crossed the boundary between the 20th and 21st centuries, decades of doomsday predictions — that computer systems storing years as two digits would interpret "00" as 1900 and crash vital infrastructure — largely failed to materialize. An estimated $300 billion had been spent worldwide on remediation code. Whether the peaceful transition vindicated the expense or exposed it as overblown remains contested.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 2000 — New Zealand and Pacific islands hit midnight first, without incident. Actual bugs did occur — a French meteorological satellite briefly misreported dates, some slot machines froze, a few nuclear plants had cooling-monitor glitches — but nothing catastrophic. The fix, written in COBOL in the 1990s, may be the largest software project ever.

events.title: Bitcoin Whitepaper Published
events.blurb: A nine-page academic paper titled "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System," written under a pseudonym, was posted to a cryptography mailing list in the middle of the global financial crisis. It described a digital currency that didn't need banks or central authorities to verify transactions. The first block of the currency was mined two months later; the identity of its author has never been established.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 2008 — "Satoshi Nakamoto." The genesis block, mined January 3, 2009, contained the text "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks" from that day's Times. Suspected Satoshis have included Hal Finney, Nick Szabo, Craig Wright (contested), and Dorian Nakamoto (denied).

events.title: Street Fighter II Released in Arcades
events.blurb: Eight distinct fighters, each with their own special moves activated by precise joystick motions, turned a local arcade into a public arena. Players lined their quarters on the cabinet bezel to declare "next game." The fighting game genre was born, arcade revenues spiked, and a competitive meta-game of frame-perfect inputs arose organically.
events.revealBlurb: February–March 1991 — Street Fighter II: The World Warrior released in North American arcades February 6 and in Japan March 7. The SNES port sold 6.3 million copies. The game is credited with single-handedly reviving the arcade industry.

events.title: Halo: Combat Evolved Launches with Xbox
events.blurb: Microsoft needed a reason for anyone to buy its new video game console from a software company. A science-fiction shooter about a soldier in powered armour became that reason. It sold one million copies faster than any console game in history, perfected twin-stick controller shooting, and made Xbox Live into the template for every online console service that followed.
events.revealBlurb: November 15, 2001 — Halo: Combat Evolved launched as a launch title for the original Xbox. Bungie had originally developed it as a Mac/PC real-time strategy game before Microsoft acquired the studio.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Minecraft Officially Released
events.blurb: A game with no story, no tutorial, no win state, and graphics that looked like 1989 asked players to punch trees and build whatever they wanted. It became the best-selling video game of all time. Schools adopted it as an educational tool. A generation learned their first lessons about architecture, resource management, and server administration inside it.
events.revealBlurb: November 18, 2011 — Minecraft version 1.0.0 launched at Minecon in Las Vegas. Microsoft acquired developer Mojang in 2014 for $2.5 billion. By 2025 the game had sold over 350 million copies — more than twice the second-best-selling game.

events.title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Released
events.blurb: A cowboy open-world game with a 60-hour main story, simulated beard growth, morality consequences for every interaction, and a horse whose bond with the player affected its responsiveness opened the largest weekend in entertainment history. It earned $725 million in three days.
events.revealBlurb: October 26, 2018 — Red Dead Redemption 2 launched for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One. It shipped 17 million copies in its first thirteen days. The game has now sold over 79 million copies. Development reportedly involved teams working 100-hour weeks across five years.

events.title: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Persian polymath in Central Asia completed a five-volume medical encyclopedia synthesizing Greek, Roman, Indian, and Islamic medical knowledge into a single coherent system, with detailed descriptions of diseases, treatments, and pharmaceuticals. Translated into Latin by the 12th century, it became the standard medical textbook of European universities for over five centuries, remaining in use into the early 1700s.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1025 — Ibn Sina (Avicenna). His synthesis included the role of preventive medicine, the value of controlled trials, and notable observations on tuberculosis and diabetes. The Canon's authority in European medical schools lasted longer than Galen's, persisting well into the Enlightenment.

events.title: Nightingale at Scutari
events.blurb: A 34-year-old British nurse arrived with 38 volunteer nurses at a filthy military hospital in a former Turkish barracks outside a Bosphorus capital, where British wounded from a Crimean war were dying of typhus, cholera, and dysentery at far higher rates than from combat wounds. Her reforms — sanitation, proper food, hand-washing, laundry — cut the death rate from 42 percent to 2 percent in six months. Her subsequent statistical advocacy reshaped nursing as a profession.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1854 — Florence Nightingale at Scutari (now Üsküdar, Istanbul). Her nighttime rounds with an oil lamp produced the "Lady with the Lamp" sobriquet. She returned to London with chronic brucellosis, spent most of the rest of her life bedridden, and still wrote 200 books and reports. She lived to 90.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine
events.blurb: A 62-year-old French chemist, who had been working for years on vaccines against animal diseases, administered his experimental rabies vaccine — desiccated spinal cord tissue from infected rabbits — to a 9-year-old Alsatian boy who had been savaged by a rabid dog two days earlier. The boy received 13 injections over ten days and survived. Rabies, previously universally fatal once symptoms appeared, now had an effective post-exposure prophylaxis.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1885 — Louis Pasteur; patient was Joseph Meister. Pasteur was not licensed as a physician; he could have been prosecuted if the boy had died. Meister grew up, became the gatekeeper at the Institut Pasteur, and is said to have killed himself in 1940 rather than let Nazi troops enter Pasteur's tomb (disputed; he may have died from gas poisoning unrelated).

events.title: HIV Identified
events.blurb: A research team at a Paris institute published a paper in the journal Science describing a new retrovirus, isolated from a lymph node of a patient with lymphadenopathy, which they believed to be the cause of AIDS. A parallel American team would publish a similar finding a year later; the credit dispute between the labs lasted years and contributed to delayed public health responses. The virus had probably crossed into humans from chimpanzees in central Africa in the early 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1983 — Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier at Institut Pasteur. Robert Gallo at the US National Cancer Institute made a similar claim in 1984. The French were eventually credited as discoverers and won the 2008 Nobel. 40 million people have died of AIDS; antiretroviral therapy since 1996 has made it a manageable chronic disease.

events.title: Licinian-Sextian Laws
events.blurb: After a decade of plebeian obstruction that left Rome with no consuls at all, the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus forced through three laws: one relieving debt, one limiting landholding to 500 iugera, and one requiring that at least one consul each year be a plebeian. Lucius Sextius duly became the first plebeian consul in 366 BCE.
events.revealBlurb: 367 BCE, Rome. Licinius and Sextius blocked every other piece of legislation for ten straight years to force the patricians to negotiate — essentially inventing the political hostage tactic of governmental gridlock.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Diocletian's Tetrarchy
events.blurb: Recognising that one man could not govern and defend an empire stretching from Scotland to Mesopotamia, Emperor Diocletian formalised a system of four co-rulers — two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars — each commanding a quarter of the empire from a frontier capital. He also doubled the size of the army, reformed the tax system, and set maximum prices for hundreds of goods.
events.revealBlurb: 293 CE. Diocletian is the only Roman emperor to voluntarily abdicate and retire — he went to grow cabbages in his palace at Split (modern Croatia). When colleagues urged him to return, he reportedly replied that if they could see the cabbages he had grown, they would not ask.

events.title: Constantine's Vision at the Milvian Bridge
events.blurb: On the eve of battle against the usurper Maxentius, Constantine reported a vision of a cross of light above the sun with the words "by this sign, conquer." He ordered the Chi-Rho symbol painted on his soldiers' shields; the following day his forces drove Maxentius's army into the Tiber, where Maxentius drowned in his armour. Constantine became sole ruler of the western empire.
events.revealBlurb: October 28, 312 CE. The battle was fought immediately outside Rome — at a bridge over the Tiber. Maxentius had broken the bridge to slow Constantine's advance, then crossed on a pontoon bridge that collapsed beneath him. A man who destroyed his own escape route to stop his enemy fell through the gap he made.

events.title: Permanent Division of the Roman Empire
events.blurb: On his deathbed in Mediolanum, Emperor Theodosius divided the empire between his two sons: eighteen-year-old Arcadius took the east with Constantinople, and ten-year-old Honorius took the west with its capital at Ravenna. No mechanism existed to reunite the two halves, and none ever did.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 395 CE. Theodosius was the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire. His ten-year-old western heir Honorius grew up to be a notably passive emperor; later historians note that when told "Rome has fallen," he reportedly burst into tears — then relaxed when he learned it was the city, not his favourite hen, also named "Rome."

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: Confederate Attack on Fort Sumter
events.blurb: At 4:30 in the morning, Confederate artillery opened fire on the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, beginning a 34-hour bombardment that forced the Union to surrender and formally launched the deadliest war in American history. No one was killed in the bombardment itself — two Union soldiers died in a cannon accident during the surrender ceremony.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1861 — Charleston, South Carolina. The Confederacy fired over 4,000 shells at the fort; Union defenders fired roughly 1,000 back. Nobody died in combat during the entire engagement. Within four days, President Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers, and four more states seceded to join the Confederacy.

events.title: Wall Street Crash: Black Tuesday
events.blurb: On the 29th of that month, stock markets collapsed in a cascade of panic selling that wiped out an estimated $14 billion in a single day, erasing the paper fortunes of thousands of investors and devastating the banking system. The crash followed years of rampant speculation fueled by easy credit and margin buying, in which millions of Americans had purchased stocks with borrowed money against collateral that suddenly no longer existed.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1929 — New York Stock Exchange. More than 16 million shares traded on Black Tuesday — a record that stood for decades. The Dow lost nearly 50% of its value by mid-November. Economists still debate whether the crash caused the Great Depression or merely triggered an underlying structural collapse.

events.title: House Impeaches President Clinton
events.blurb: The House of Representatives voted to impeach President Bill Clinton on the 19th of that month, on charges of perjury before a grand jury (228–206) and obstruction of justice (221–212) arising from his false testimony about a sexual relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Clinton became only the second U.S. president ever to be impeached; the Senate acquitted him on both articles the following February.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1998 — U.S. Capitol. The vote occurred while U.S. warplanes were bombing Iraq (Operation Desert Fox), which the White House denied was timed to distract from the impeachment. House Speaker-designate Bob Livingston resigned that same day. Clinton's approval rating on the day of his impeachment was 73%.

events.title: Barack Obama Elected President
events.blurb: A first-term U.S. senator, 47 years old and the son of a Kenyan father and Kansan mother, defeated his Republican opponent by a nine-million-vote margin to become the 44th President of the United States and the first Black person elected to the office. He carried states no Democrat had won in decades, including Indiana and North Carolina.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 2008 — defeating John McCain. Obama gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park before 200,000 people. Jesse Jackson, standing in the crowd, wept on camera. Michelle Obama became the first African-American First Lady.

events.title: First Animal in Earth Orbit
events.blurb: A stray mixed-breed dog named Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, a 508 kg spacecraft with no reentry capability. Laika survived liftoff and initial orbit but died from overheating within five to seven hours when a thermal regulation system failed — a fact withheld from the public for decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1957 — Sputnik 2. The Soviets announced Laika died painlessly after several days; the truth wasn't confirmed until 2002. The spacecraft had been built in under four weeks on Khrushchev's orders to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution. Laika has since been honored with a monument in Moscow and a postage stamp in more than 70 countries.

events.title: Explorer 1 — First US Satellite
events.blurb: A Juno I rocket launched the United States' first satellite from Cape Canaveral, placing an 8.3 kg cylinder into an elliptical orbit that reached 2,550 km altitude. The satellite's Geiger–Müller tube detected a region of intense radiation surrounding Earth — data that led James Van Allen to identify the radiation belts bearing his name.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1958 — Explorer 1. The US had been beaten to orbit by Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2 in the previous three months. In a press conference photo, three scientists hoisted a full-scale model over their heads in triumph — the actual satellite weighed less than a toaster oven. Explorer 1 remained in orbit for 12 years.

events.title: First Crewed Lunar Orbit
events.blurb: Three astronauts fired their Service Propulsion System engine on Christmas Eve to enter orbit 112 km above the Moon — the first humans to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and orbit another world. During the mission's ninth orbit, Bill Anders photographed a crescent Earth rising over the lunar horizon, producing what became one of the most widely reproduced photographs in history.
events.revealBlurb: December 24, 1968 — Apollo 8. An estimated one billion people across 64 countries watched the Christmas Eve television broadcast in which the crew read the opening verses of Genesis. The Earthrise photograph is credited with catalyzing the environmental movement; the image appeared on the first Earth Day poster in 1970.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: ISS First Crewed Occupation
events.blurb: A three-person crew docked a Soyuz capsule to the International Space Station's Zvezda module at 09:21 UTC, beginning a continuous human presence in low Earth orbit that has not been interrupted since. The station at that point consisted of three connected modules spanning roughly 27 meters, a fraction of its eventual 109-meter length.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 2000 — Expedition 1. Commander Bill Shepherd radioed NASA to request the station's call sign be changed from "Alpha" to "International Space Station" — a small act of diplomacy that stuck. The crew of two Russians and one American had access to less than 425 cubic meters of living space, about the volume of a large school bus.

events.title: Luther Posts the 95 Theses
events.blurb: A 33-year-old German university theologian sent his local archbishop a letter enclosing a 95-point list of academic propositions challenging the papal indulgence system — the practice of selling forgiveness of sins. By tradition, he also posted the Latin theses on the door of his university church, which served as a community bulletin board. Copies reached print within weeks and spread across Germany. He had intended academic debate; he ignited the Protestant Reformation.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1517 — Martin Luther at Wittenberg Castle Church. Most scholars doubt the physical nailing-to-the-door story; the letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz is well-documented. October 31 is now celebrated as Reformation Day in many Protestant countries.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Henry VIII Breaks with Rome
events.blurb: An English parliament passed an Act of Supremacy declaring the king — who had wanted for years to annul his marriage to a Spanish princess who had given him no male heir, and whom the pope had refused — the "Supreme Head" of the Church of England. The break with Rome was not primarily theological; the king remained Catholic in doctrine for the rest of his life. It rewrote England's religious, political, and property landscape for the next century.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1534 — Henry VIII. He had already married Anne Boleyn (his second wife) in secret in January 1533. The archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, had annulled his first marriage in May. Henry would have six wives; two were beheaded, two divorced, one died in childbirth.

events.title: St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre
events.blurb: A coordinated series of assassinations of French Protestant leaders in the capital, authorized by the king on the advice of his Italian-born mother, expanded within hours into uncontrolled mob violence against the Protestant population. The killings spread to provincial cities over the following weeks. Death-toll estimates range from 5,000 to 30,000. The massacre marked the effective end of Huguenot political power in France for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1572 — the feast of Saint Bartholomew. Catherine de' Medici was queen mother to King Charles IX. The Protestant leader Admiral de Coligny was thrown from a window and his body mutilated. The Pope ordered a Te Deum of thanksgiving in Rome and had a commemorative medal struck.

events.title: Spanish Armada Defeated
events.blurb: A Spanish naval force of 130 ships and 26,000 men, intended to escort a Flemish invasion army across the Channel to England, was met by a faster, more maneuverable English fleet off the Flanders coast. An English fireship attack scattered the Spanish anchorage overnight; the following day's running battle crippled the armada. Storms in the North Sea and along the Irish coast destroyed the rest on the long retreat home. Barely half returned to Spain.
events.revealBlurb: July 29 to August 8, 1588 — Battle of Gravelines decided it. English commanders: Lord Howard of Effingham, Sir Francis Drake. Roughly 35 Spanish ships reached home; most of the rest were wrecked on the Irish coast, whose people dealt harshly with survivors.
